Plainchants were religious single line melodies sung in churches.
They were always sung a cappella (N5).
Plainchant music is always sung in Latin.

The Baroque period in music, art, architecture, and fashion was fancy, highly detailed and ornamented.
Theatre, opera and music were important to the rich monarchies and nobility of Europe, and a lot of music was composed for performances in palaces and courts.
Religious music was also important in this era, with composers such as Bach writing huge amounts of music for use in church.

The harpsichord was a popular keyboard instrument in the Baroque period, with its distinctive plucked sound.
Another popular keyboard instrument in baroque music is the pipe organ. In some pieces you may hear an organ playing along with the strings instead of the harpsichord.
The recorder is a woodwind instrument which was popular in the Baroque period and came in many different sizes.
The strings were very important in the Baroque period.

A trill is a rapid alternation between two notes next to each other. A trill is a type of ornament (N4) which is a way to decorate a melody.
A mordent is an ornament which quickly sounds the main note, the note above or below and then the main note again.
An acciaccatura is an ornament which sounds like a crushed note, played very quickly on the beat or just before it.
Although lots of ornaments were used in Baroque music, they were not exclusive to Baroque music.

paragraphs: From 1450 to 1600, Europe experienced a period of exploration in art, music, science, and learning.
This era, known as the Renaissance, was a time of rebirth, drawing inspiration from ancient Greek and Roman cultures.

Artists created more realistic paintings, musicians wrote richer harmonies, and inventors made groundbreaking discoveries. The Renaissance fostered creativity and curiosity, transforming people’s perception of the world.
Historical instruments – lute, viol, recorder and crumhorn are commonly used.
Sacred and secular music – motets and anthems sit alongside madrigals and dances.
Polyphonic texture – several independent melodies are heard at the same time.
Modal harmony – music is often based on modes rather than modern major/minor keys.
A cappella singing – vocal music performed without instrumental accompaniment.
Imitation – one voice or part copies a melody introduced by another.

During this period, composers started to explore a variety of different textures and styles:
The motet is a short sacred choral work, usually polyphonic in texture, with a Latin text. It is sung a cappella.
O How Glorious is the Kingdom
The anthem is a short sacred choral piece which often features often features solo parts.
It may be sung a cappella or with organ accompaniment.

The ayre (or song) was often performed by a solo voice, accompanied by either lute or viol.

Sung in English with lyrical, expressive melody.
A countertenor is the highest male voice.
In early music, higher voices were associated with goodness and purity, while low, natural men’s voices evoked evil or corruption.
Because of this, many heroic male roles were written for high male voices.

From around 1600 to 1750, Europe entered a period of drama, contrast, and elaborate artistic expression.This era, known as the Baroque period, saw artists, architects, and musicians create works designed to impress and stir emotion.Music became more expressive, with strong contrasts, ornamented melodies, basso continuo, and the development of forms such as opera and the concerto.
Instruments – harpsichord, organ, violin, cello and recorder are commonly used.
Major and minor keys – music increasingly uses the major/minor tonal system rather than modes.
Basso continuo – a continuous bass line supports the harmony, often played by harpsichord or organ with a bass instrument.
Ornamentation – melodies are decorated with trills, mordents and other embellishments.
Terraced dynamics – sudden changes between loud and soft are common rather than gradual changes.
Polyphonic texture and imitation – several independent parts are often combined, especially in fugues and contrapuntal music.

They typically have a homophonic texture

A rhythmic device often at cadence points where accents shift to create the impression of a time change.
It makes music in triple time sound like duple time or the reverse.
If you struggle hearing it then just think of it as a fancy time change.

Play the main note, the note above or below and then the main note again quickly.

An appoggiatura is an ornament that uses a non-chord note in a melody that resolves to the regular chord note.
Placing it on a strong beat emphasizes the appoggiatura, delaying the expected chord note.
A turn is an ornament consisting of three notes where you play the note above, main note, note below, main note.

The entire fugue would generally be based on a single melodic idea called the subject.

The subject would be first heard in one voice only and then imitated by the other voices in turn - this is called the answer.

The accordion has a keyboard played with the right hand and buttons pressed by the left hand. The sound is produced by bellows, also operated with the left hand.
An Irish wooden drum, held in one hand and played with a wooden beater called a tipper.
Clarsach is Gaelic for "harp“. This is slightly smaller than the orchestral harp but functions the same way.
Scotland’s national instrument, played by blowing the bag full of air and pushing it out. Bagpipes feature a drone.

paragraphs: Music written for a small ensemble, usually with one player on each part. It was traditionally performed in a smaller room rather than a large concert hall.
•  Ensemble size — small group of musicians.
•  Parts — one player performs each part.
•  Examples — trios, quartets, quintets and other small ensembles.
•  Listening clue — individual lines and instrumental timbres can often be heard clearly.
A chamber group containing two violins, one viola and one cello. String quartets were popular in the Classical and Romantic periods; Haydn wrote 68.
A chamber group consisting of piano, violin and cello. Each part is of equal importance. It is one of the most common groups in Classical and Romantic chamber music.
String quartet — four bowed string parts; no piano.

Schubert: The Fair Maid of the Mill
Performed by a solo singer, usually a tenor, and pianist.
A cycle of 20 songs; around half are in strophic form.
Based on a love story that moves from cheerful optimism to despair and tragedy.
The songs are linked by a common story and poetic source.
A short recurring musical theme associated with a particular character, object, place, emotion or plot element.
Wagner used leitmotifs to help organise long dramatic works and connect music with the story.
•  Characters — for example a hero or other named figure.
•  Objects — for example a ring or sword.
•  Places — for example a river, home or landscape.
•  Emotions or ideas — for example love, destiny or death.
A leitmotif may return in different keys, tempos, dynamics, rhythms or timbres to reflect the changing mood or action.

Music that expresses a strong connection with a composer's country or national identity. Nationalist ideas became especially significant during the 19th century.

•  Stories, legends, historical events or national heroes.

•  Distinctive instruments, scales, rhythms or styles associated with a culture.

Jean Sibelius, a Romantic-period Finnish composer, played an important role in the formation of Finnish national identity. His symphonic poem Finlandia was composed in response to censorship imposed by the Russian Empire. Its rousing, turbulent music came to symbolise the Finnish national struggle.

A triad is chord containing three notes. In root position, major and minor triads are built from scale degrees 1, 3 and 5.
A major triad with an added sixth above the root. This chord is used frequently in jazz and popular music.
A major triad plus a minor seventh, built on scale degree 5. It often resolves to the tonic and may form a perfect cadence (V–I).
A four-note chord built from stacked minor thirds. The interval from root to seventh is a diminished seventh, creating a strongly dissonant sound.
A major triad with a raised fifth. The raised fifth creates an unstable, dissonant sound and often moves by semitone to a note in the following chord.
Compare a major triad with an augmented triad: the raised fifth produces the distinctive unsettled colour.
Listen for chromatic semitone movement when the chord resolves.
An interval of three whole tones, for example C to F♯. It may also be described as an augmented fourth or diminished fifth, depending on its spelling.
Its dissonant sound was handled carefully in earlier tonal music and used more freely by many later composers.
The interval is also contained within a dominant seventh chord and contributes to its need to resolve.

Important composers of the Classical period include:
Classical music has a lighter, clearer texture than Baroque music and is less complex. It is mainly homophonic, using a clear singable melody line.

The orchestra in the Classical period now featured the addition of the flute, oboe, the recently invented clarinet, and the bassoon, along with a couple of French horns.
The harpsichord was replaced as the main keyboard instrument by the piano.

Chamber music is music written to be performed by a small group of musicians, in a small room rather than in a big hall.
In a chamber ensemble only one musician plays each part.
Common chamber music ensembles include trios, quartets, quintets and octets.
These are usually made up of related instruments e.g. a wind quintet of flute, oboe, clarinet, French horn and bassoon.
A string quartet is a chamber ensemble, containing two violins, one viola and one cello.

paragraphs: Tempo is the speed of the music. We use Italian terms to describe tempo.
The tempo marking is written above the first bar of the music.

An anacrusis is where the melody starts on the last beat of the bar.
A pause is when the music momentarily stops. On the music, there will be a pause marking above the note.
Tonality is the mood of a piece of music.

In music, a scale is a unique pattern of tones (N5) and semitones (N5). Each scale has its own distinctive sound.

A cadence is formed by two chords at the end of a passage of music.
There are two cadences you should know of:
Perfect cadences sound as though the music has come to an end – a full stop.
A perfect cadence is formed by the chords V - I.
Imperfect cadences sound like the music hasn’t finished – like a comma.
An imperfect cadence ends on chord V.

An ornament is a way to decorate the melody to make it sound more interesting.
A trill is a rapid alternation between two notes which are next to each other.
Grace notes are played quickly, “crushed” before the main note. They are often found in Scottish music.

Key changes happen towards the end of pop songs

An octave is when you leap from one letter to the same letter 8 notes higher or lower. For example, low C to high C.

Form describes the structure of a piece of music – beginning, middle, and end.
Binary form divides into two clear sections.
We generally refer to these sections as section A and section B. Each section is often repeated.
Ternary form divides into three clear sections.
We still call these sections A and B. The difference with ternary form, however, is that section A comes back again at the end.
In a rondo, the first section (A) keeps coming back in between different sections – B, C etc. These different sections are known as episodes.

paragraphs: The Baroque period in music, art, architecture, and fashion was fancy, highly detailed and ornamented.
The harpsichord was a popular keyboard instrument in the Baroque period, with its distinctive plucked sound.
Another popular keyboard instrument in baroque music is the pipe organ. In some pieces you may hear an organ playing along with the strings instead of the harpsichord.
The recorder is a woodwind instrument which was popular in the Baroque period and came in many different sizes.
The strings were very important in the Baroque period. The other sections of the orchestra had not yet become fully established.

A sequence is a pattern of notes repeating at a higher or lower pitch.
A trill is a rapid alternation between two notes next to each other. A trill is a type of ornament (N4) which is a way to decorate a melody.
A grace note is another ornament you’ve already learned about.

The Classical period in music, art, architecture and fashion valued balance, symmetry, and classiness. Architecture became simpler than in the Baroque period, with clean, symmetrical shapes and columns.
Classical music has a lighter, clearer texture than Baroque music and is less complex. It is mainly homophonic, using a clear singable melody line.
The harpsichord was replaced as the main keyboard instrument by the piano.
In a broken chord, the notes of a chord are played separately.

The orchestra in the Classical period now featured the addition of the flute, oboe, the recently invented clarinet, and the bassoon, along with a couple of French horns.
The symphony is a large-scale work for the full orchestra.
A coda is a passage at the end of a piece of music which rounds it off effectively. This usually applies to large orchestral works like the symphony.
A concerto is a large-scale work for a solo instrument accompanied by an orchestra.
There were many concertos composed throughout the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods.

An important feature of a concerto is the cadenza - a passage of music which allows the soloist to display their technical ability on their instrument. It is played without orchestral accompaniment and often ends with a trill, as a signal to the orchestra to play again.
